subject: biology

items.q: Part of the base sequence of a gene is GAT TCA GGC ATT before a mutation and GAT TCG GCA TT after it. Which type of gene mutation has occurred?
items.correct: A deletion of one base, which has moved every later base one position along
items.misconception: A substitution of the base A by G at the sixth position in the sequence
items.why: Substitution is the first mutation type students meet, and they compare sequences base by base at each position rather than sliding one sequence along to align it. A shift of one place then looks like many bases having been swapped. Substitution, insertion and deletion are distinguished by comparing the aligned sequences and their lengths. A substitution leaves the length unchanged and alters one base; an insertion or deletion changes the length and displaces every base after the mutation point, so many positions appear different even though only one base was added or lost.
items.specStatementText: Three kinds of gene mutation: substitution, insertion, deletion
items.random_wrong: A chromosome mutation, because the total amount of DNA has changed

items.q: In mRNA the codons GCU, GCC, GCA and GCG all code for alanine. A base substitution in a gene changes the codon GCU in its mRNA to GCC. What is the effect on the polypeptide?
items.correct: None: the same amino acid, alanine, is placed at that position
items.misconception: Alanine is replaced by a different amino acid at that one position
items.why: Students learn that each codon codes for one amino acid and treat the relationship as one-to-one, forgetting that most amino acids have several codons. GCSE-level accounts of mutation usually describe substitutions that do change an amino acid. Most amino acids are specified by two or more codons. A substitution, especially in the third base of a codon, often produces a different codon for the same amino acid, so the polypeptide is unchanged. Substitutions may or may not change a single amino acid.
items.specStatementText: A substitution may change one amino acid, or none
items.random_wrong: The reading frame shifts, changing all amino acids after it

items.q: The same gene was sequenced in 1000 people. At one position 62% carry C and 38% carry T, and the two resulting codons code for the same amino acid. How should this difference be described?
items.correct: An SNP that leaves the polypeptide unchanged
items.misconception: A rare mutation causing disease in the 38% group
items.why: Mutation is introduced alongside genetic disease, so students hear polymorphism as another word for a defective gene. The SNPs quoted in the media are usually those linked to disease risk. SNPs are the result of base substitution mutations that have spread in a population and are now variants carried by many individuals. Because of the degeneracy of the genetic code, an SNP within a gene may or may not change a single amino acid, and most SNPs have no known effect on health.
items.specStatementText: A substitution may change one amino acid, or none
items.random_wrong: A frameshift mutation that affects later codons

items.q: One base is deleted from the fourth codon of a gene coding for a polypeptide of 300 amino acids. What is the most likely consequence?
items.correct: Almost all of the polypeptide is altered and it ceases to function
items.misconception: Only the fourth amino acid is altered, so the polypeptide still works normally
items.why: Students apply the rule they learned for substitutions (one base, one codon, one amino acid) to every type of mutation, and picture the deleted base as leaving a gap in one codon rather than as pulling every later base along by one place. Bases are read in groups of three from a fixed starting point. Removing one base moves every later base one position up, so all the codons after the deletion are regrouped and read differently: this is a frameshift, and the polypeptide from that point on is changed and is likely to cease to function.
items.specStatementText: Insertions and deletions usually wreck the polypeptide
items.random_wrong: Every one of the 300 amino acids is changed, including the first three

items.q: Two copies of a gene are mutated at the same point in the coding sequence. In copy X three consecutive bases are inserted; in copy Y one base is inserted. Which comparison is correct?
items.correct: X keeps the reading frame so the codons after it are unchanged, but Y shifts the frame for every later codon
items.misconception: Both X and Y shift the reading frame, so both of the polypeptides are likely to cease to function
items.why: Frameshift is taught as the consequence of insertions and deletions, and the qualifying condition (a number of bases that is not a multiple of three) is easily dropped. Examples given in class are nearly always single-base changes. The frame shifts only when the number of bases inserted or deleted is not a multiple of three. An insertion or deletion of three bases (or six, nine and so on) adds or removes whole codons, so one or a few amino acids are gained or lost but the rest of the polypeptide is unchanged.
items.specStatementText: Insertions and deletions usually wreck the polypeptide
items.random_wrong: Both X and Y alter just one amino acid at the insertion point, leaving the rest unchanged

items.q: Why is a polypeptide likely to cease functioning when several hundred bases are deleted from the middle of its gene?
items.correct: So many amino acids are missing that the polypeptide cannot fold into its working shape
items.misconception: The amino acids coded before the deletion are also changed by the loss of bases
items.why: Students hear that a frameshift changes the whole polypeptide and do not connect this with the direction of reading. They picture the mRNA as reshuffled all along its length rather than as shifted from one point onwards. The ribosome reads codons from the start codon in order, so the frame is correct until it reaches the mutation. From the point of the insertion or deletion onwards, every codon is regrouped and the amino acid sequence changes; the sequence before that point is unaffected.
items.specStatementText: Insertions and deletions usually wreck the polypeptide
items.random_wrong: Only because a deletion of any size shifts the reading frame of every later codon

items.q: Which statement about the causes of gene mutation is correct?
items.correct: Replication errors can cause mutation without a mutagen
items.misconception: Gene mutations arise only in cells that are exposed to a mutagen
items.why: Mutagens are the named, visible causes of mutation in every textbook and public-health message, whereas replication errors are invisible and rare, so students conclude that mutation requires an external cause. Gene mutation can be caused by mutagens and by errors in DNA replication or repair. DNA polymerase occasionally inserts the wrong base and repair enzymes occasionally fail to correct it, so a low background rate of mutation exists in every dividing cell regardless of exposure to mutagens.
items.specStatementText: Mutagens, and copying errors, cause mutation
items.random_wrong: Microwaves and radio waves are mutagenic just like X-rays

items.q: Cultures of cells were exposed separately to (i) ultraviolet light, (ii) visible light and (iii) nitrous acid, a chemical that alters bases in DNA. Which treatments are expected to raise the mutation rate above the background rate?
items.correct: (i) and (iii), because both chemically alter the bases in DNA
items.misconception: (i), (ii) and (iii), because light and chemicals both damage DNA
items.why: The everyday word radiation is attached to anything that is emitted or transmitted, and media stories about phone masts and microwaves suggest that all of it damages cells. Students do not distinguish ionizing and ultraviolet radiation from lower-energy radiation. Only radiation with enough energy to break bonds in DNA or alter its bases is mutagenic. Ionizing radiation and ultraviolet light are mutagenic; visible light, microwaves and radio waves are not, because they cannot cause chemical changes to DNA.
items.specStatementText: Mutagens, and copying errors, cause mutation
items.random_wrong: (iii) only, because radiation from non-radioactive sources is harmless

items.q: Which statement about randomness in mutation is correct?
items.correct: Mutations can occur anywhere in the genome, but some bases have a higher probability of mutating than others
items.misconception: Mutations can occur anywhere in the genome, and every base has an identical probability of mutating
items.why: Random is understood in its everyday sense of 'equally likely', so students merge two separate ideas: that mutation is not directed towards usefulness, and that all sites are equally likely to change. Randomness in mutation means that which base changes is not determined by whether the change would be beneficial. It does not mean uniform probability: the chemistry of particular bases and sequences makes some positions in a genome mutation hotspots with a much higher probability of mutating than others.
items.specStatementText: Mutation is random, but not evenly spread
items.random_wrong: Mutations occur in the genes an organism needs to change when its environment changes

items.q: A bacterial culture that has never been exposed to the antibiotic streptomycin is found to contain about one resistant cell per 10⁷ cells. When streptomycin is added, the resistant cells survive and the culture soon consists almost entirely of resistant cells. What do these observations show?
items.correct: The resistance mutation arose by chance before exposure, and the antibiotic then selected the cells carrying it
items.misconception: The antibiotic caused the bacteria to mutate the gene that gives resistance because they needed it in order to survive
items.why: Everyday language says that bacteria 'develop' or 'become' resistant, and evolutionary change is often described as a response to the environment, so students infer that the environment directs which mutation occurs. It is a Lamarckian idea that survives from primary and middle-school accounts of adaptation. Mutations can occur anywhere in the base sequences of a genome and are not directed towards a useful outcome. A resistance mutation may already be present, having arisen by chance before the antibiotic was applied; the antibiotic then selects the cells that carry it. Natural selection, not directed mutation, produces the adaptation.
items.specStatementText: Mutation is random, but not evenly spread
items.random_wrong: Most mutations in bacteria are beneficial, which is why the resistance spread through the culture so quickly

items.q: Which statement about mutations in germ cells and somatic cells is correct?
items.correct: A mutation in a germ cell can be passed on to the offspring
items.misconception: A mutation in a skin cell can be inherited by the person's children
items.why: Students think of a person's DNA as a single thing, so a change anywhere in the body is a change to 'their genes' that will be inherited. The distinction between the germ line and the rest of the body is new at this level. Only genes in gametes are transmitted to offspring. A mutation in a somatic cell is copied into that cell's descendants within the individual and dies with the individual; a mutation in a germ cell can be inherited and will then be present in every cell of the offspring.
items.specStatementText: Germ cell mutations are inherited; somatic mutations stay in the body
items.random_wrong: Every mutation in a somatic cell causes that cell to become cancerous

items.q: A mutation occurs in a gene that controls the cell cycle in one cell lining a man's colon. Which statement about the consequences is correct?
items.correct: The cell may divide uncontrollably and form a tumour
items.misconception: The mutation will spread to every cell in the man's body
items.why: Inherited mutations are indeed present in every cell, because they were in the zygote, and students transfer this to mutations that arise later. They may also picture DNA being shared between cells rather than copied only at cell division. A mutation is copied only when the cell that carries it replicates its DNA and divides. A somatic mutation is therefore confined to a clone of cells descended from the original mutant cell; it is present in every cell of the body only if it occurred in the zygote or was inherited through a gamete.
items.specStatementText: Germ cell mutations are inherited; somatic mutations stay in the body
items.random_wrong: The mutation will be passed on to all of the man's children

items.q: Why is gene mutation described as the original source of all genetic variation?
items.correct: New alleles arise only by mutation; meiosis and fertilization just recombine alleles that already exist
items.misconception: Crossing over in meiosis creates new alleles, and mutation adds to the variation they produce
items.why: Meiosis and fertilization are taught as sources of genetic variation, and students do not separate variation in combinations of alleles from variation in the alleles themselves. Crossing over is pictured as making new genes rather than reshuffling old ones. Gene mutation is the original source of all genetic variation: it is the only process that produces a new allele. Meiosis and fertilization generate new combinations of alleles that already exist, which is a different level of variation.
items.specStatementText: Mutation is where all new alleles come from
items.random_wrong: Most mutations are beneficial, so each one adds a useful new variant to the species

items.q: A direct-to-consumer genetic test reports that a healthy woman carries an SNP associated with a risk of type 2 diabetes 1.5 times higher than that of people without it. Which interpretation is correct?
items.correct: She is more likely than non-carriers to develop the disease, but may never do so; expert interpretation is needed
items.misconception: She will certainly develop type 2 diabetes in later life, because she carries the genetic variant that causes the disease
items.why: Genetics is introduced through single-gene conditions in which genotype determines phenotype, so students expect all genetic results to be deterministic. The word risk is read as a prediction rather than as a probability. Commercial genetic tests yield information about potential future health and disease risk, not certainties. Most variants tested are SNPs associated with a modest change in probability, and without expert interpretation of what the probability means the information can be problematic, causing unnecessary alarm or false reassurance.
items.specStatementText: Mutation is where all new alleles come from
items.random_wrong: The test has diagnosed type 2 diabetes in her, so she should begin treatment for the disease immediately

items.q: Researchers want to investigate the function of gene Z in mice. They obtain a strain from a knockout library in which gene Z is inoperative. How should they use it?
items.correct: Compare the phenotype of the knockout mice with that of normal mice
items.misconception: Conclude that Z has no function if the knockout mice appear normal
items.why: The logic of the technique is presented as 'remove the gene and see what is lost', and students take the absence of a visible change at face value. They are not yet aware of gene redundancy or of the limits of what a laboratory phenotype records. A knockout gives evidence about gene function only when a phenotype changes. No change can mean that a second gene with a similar product masks the loss, that the function is needed only in conditions not tested (for example stress, infection or old age), or that the difference is too subtle to detect, so a null result does not show that the gene is functionless.
items.specStatementText: Knock a gene out to see what it does
items.random_wrong: Check first that the whole of gene Z has been cut out of the chromosome

items.q: Mice in which gene P has been knocked out show no detectable difference from normal mice under standard laboratory conditions. What is the best conclusion?
items.correct: P may have a function masked by another gene or shown only in untested conditions
items.misconception: The knockout did not work, because the sequence of P is still present in the genome
items.why: The word knockout suggests removal, and diagrams of the genome shown with a gene missing reinforce it. Students also confuse knockout with the deletion of a gene at the chromosome level. Gene knockout is a technique for investigating the function of a gene by changing it to make it inoperative. Whether the change is a deletion, an insertion that disrupts the sequence or another alteration, what matters is that no working gene product is made, so the phenotype can be compared with that of the normal organism.
items.specStatementText: Knock a gene out to see what it does
items.random_wrong: P has no function, because removing its product produced no change in the mice's phenotype

items.q: In CRISPR–Cas9 gene editing, what determines the position in the genome at which the DNA is cut?
items.correct: The base sequence of the guide RNA, which pairs with the complementary sequence in the target DNA
items.misconception: The active site of the Cas9 enzyme, which recognises the target DNA base sequence directly
items.why: Enzymes are taught as having specificity through their active site, so students assume the enzyme must be what confers specificity here. The guide RNA is a new kind of component and its role is under-appreciated. Cas9 cuts wherever it is taken. The specificity of CRISPR–Cas9 comes from the guide RNA: its sequence of about 20 bases is designed to be complementary to the target, and base pairing between the guide RNA and the DNA holds Cas9 at that single position. Changing the guide RNA changes the target.
items.specStatementText: CRISPR–Cas9 cuts DNA where a guide RNA leads it
items.random_wrong: The guide RNA, which cuts both strands of the DNA at the position where it binds to it

items.q: Which of the following is an example of the successful use of CRISPR–Cas9 gene editing?
items.correct: Editing the blood-forming stem cells of patients with sickle cell disease so that they produce fetal haemoglobin
items.misconception: Using Cas9 itself both to cut out the faulty bases and to write the corrected sequence into the gene
items.why: The technique is described as 'editing', which in everyday use means rewriting, so students expect the tool to do the writing. Explanations often stop at the cut and leave the repair step implicit. Cas9 is only a nuclease: it makes a double-strand break. The edit is produced by the cell's DNA repair processes. Repair without a template often introduces small insertions or deletions that disrupt the gene; repair using a supplied template can incorporate a designed sequence.
items.specStatementText: CRISPR–Cas9 cuts DNA where a guide RNA leads it
items.random_wrong: Editing the skin cells of adults with sickle cell disease so that all their own children inherit the corrected gene

items.q: In 2018 a scientist announced the birth of babies whose genomes had been edited with CRISPR–Cas9 at the embryo stage. The work was condemned by scientists worldwide and the scientist was later imprisoned under his own country's laws. Why is there an international effort to harmonize the regulation of genome editing?
items.correct: Regulation is national, so a use banned in one country may be legal in another
items.misconception: A single worldwide law on genome editing exists and only needs to be enforced
items.why: Students assume that a technology with such obvious ethical weight must already be controlled by a global authority, in the way they imagine international bodies control weapons or drugs. Reports of a scientist being punished are read as proof of a world law. Regulation of research is national. A use of CRISPR that is banned in one country may be legal or unregulated in another, so scientists could move work to the least restrictive jurisdiction. This is the reason for the international effort to harmonize the regulation of genome editing technologies, which is still in progress.
items.specStatementText: CRISPR–Cas9 cuts DNA where a guide RNA leads it
items.random_wrong: Once embryo editing is shown to be safe there will be no ethical issue left to regulate

items.q: The gene for histone H4 codes for an almost identical amino acid sequence in peas and in cattle, whose lineages diverged over a billion years ago. Which pair of hypotheses could account for this?
items.correct: Selection removes mutations that impair the protein, or the gene mutates more slowly
items.misconception: The DNA of the gene is protected so that no mutation can occur in it in either organism
items.why: Conserved is heard as 'preserved from damage', and students look for a mechanism that stops the change rather than one that removes changed individuals. Selection acting on individuals is harder to picture than a sequence being left alone. Two hypotheses account for conserved sequences. One is functional requirement: mutations arise, but almost any change impairs the gene product so carriers are eliminated by natural selection and only the original sequence persists. The other is a slower rate of mutation in that region. Observing conservation alone does not tell you which applies.
items.specStatementText: Two hypotheses for why some sequences barely change
items.random_wrong: The gene is not used in either organism, so nothing has changed it since they diverged

items.q: The rate at which new mutations appear per generation was measured directly in a highly conserved gene and in a gene that is not conserved. The rates were the same, but far fewer of the new mutations in the conserved gene persisted in later generations. Which hypothesis do the data support?
items.correct: Functional requirement: mutations arise at the normal rate but carriers are removed by natural selection
items.misconception: Lack of use: the conserved gene is inactive, so mutations in it have no effect and persist
items.why: Students reason from everyday objects, where things that are used wear out and things left alone stay intact. They may also recall that much of the genome is non-coding and assume it is the unchanging part. Sequences that are not used are not protected by natural selection, so mutations in them persist and they diverge rapidly between species. A sequence that has stayed almost identical over hundreds of millions of years is one in which changes have been either prevented or strongly selected against, which points to an essential function.
items.specStatementText: Two hypotheses for why some sequences barely change
items.random_wrong: Slower mutation rate: the conserved gene is protected from mutation, so fewer changes arise in it

items.q: A gene becomes two bases shorter. Is this a gene mutation or a chromosome mutation?
items.correct: A gene mutation: a deletion within the gene's base sequence. Chromosome mutations change the number or structure of whole chromosomes.
items.misconception: Any change that alters the amount of DNA, such as an insertion or deletion, is a chromosome mutation; gene mutations are only swaps of one base for another.
items.why: Earlier courses present mutation mainly through chromosome examples (extra or missing chromosomes), and the word deletion is also used for chromosome deletions, so students sort mutations by whether DNA is gained or lost rather than by the level at which the change occurs. Gene mutations are structural changes to genes at the molecular level, and include substitutions, insertions and deletions of bases within the gene. A change in the number or structure of whole chromosomes is a chromosome mutation, which is a different category.
items.specStatementText: Three kinds of gene mutation: substitution, insertion, deletion
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a base substitution shift the reading frame of the gene?
items.correct: No. A substitution replaces one base with another, so every codon stays in the same position; only the codon containing the substituted base is altered.
items.misconception: A base substitution shifts the reading frame so that every codon after it is misread.
items.why: Frameshift is the most memorable consequence of mutation, and students attach it to any mutation rather than only to insertions and deletions. Diagrams that show a substitution and a frameshift side by side reinforce the idea that both spread down the sequence. The reading frame is set by the number of bases, read three at a time. A substitution keeps the number of bases the same, so the frame is unchanged and at most one codon (and one amino acid) is affected. Only insertions or deletions of a number of bases that is not a multiple of three cause a frameshift.
items.specStatementText: A substitution may change one amino acid, or none
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is ultraviolet light a mutagen, even though it is not emitted by radioactive materials?
items.correct: Yes. Ultraviolet light is a mutagenic form of radiation: it causes adjacent thymine bases to bond together, which leads to errors when the DNA is replicated or repaired. Chemicals such as benzo[a]pyrene in tobacco smoke are mutagens too.
items.misconception: Only radiation from radioactive sources or nuclear accidents causes mutations; sunlight and other non-nuclear radiation cannot alter genes.
items.why: Radiation is introduced in physics through radioactive decay, and the best-known mutation stories (Hiroshima, Chernobyl) involve nuclear radiation, so students narrow mutagenic radiation to that source and overlook ultraviolet light altogether. Mutagens include chemical mutagens (for example benzo[a]pyrene in tobacco smoke, nitrosamines and mustard gas) and mutagenic forms of radiation, which include ultraviolet light as well as X-rays, gamma rays and particles from radioactive isotopes. Ultraviolet light from the sun is the main cause of mutations leading to skin cancer.
items.specStatementText: Mutagens, and copying errors, cause mutation
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: DNA polymerase proofreads and cells have DNA repair enzymes. Does this mean replication errors never become mutations?
items.correct: No. Proofreading and repair correct most errors, but a small fraction escape and become permanent mutations; faults in the repair process itself can also cause mutation.
items.misconception: Because DNA replication is proofread and damage is repaired, every error is corrected and replication errors cannot be a cause of mutation.
items.why: Proofreading and repair are taught as the reason replication is so accurate, and students turn a very low error rate into a zero error rate. They also assume that repair enzymes are themselves perfect. Errors in DNA replication or repair are one of the two causes of gene mutation named in the guide. Repair reduces the mutation rate to roughly one in a billion bases per replication but does not eliminate it, and over a genome of billions of bases copied many times, unrepaired errors accumulate.
items.specStatementText: Mutagens, and copying errors, cause mutation
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does every mutation in a somatic cell cause cancer?
items.correct: No. Cancer results from mutations in the particular genes that control the cell cycle and cell division; most somatic mutations are neutral or affect other functions.
items.misconception: Any mutation in a somatic cell turns that cell into a cancer cell.
items.why: Cancer is the one consequence of somatic mutation that students are taught, so mutation in a body cell and cancer become equated. The many silent or harmless mutations that every somatic cell accumulates are never mentioned. Somatic mutations are common and most have no effect on the cell. Cancer requires mutations in genes that control the cell cycle, so that the cell escapes normal control and divides uncontrollably. Usually several such mutations must accumulate in one cell line before a tumour forms.
items.specStatementText: Germ cell mutations are inherited; somatic mutations stay in the body
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are most mutations beneficial to the organism in which they occur?
items.correct: No. Most mutations are harmful or neutral for the individual; only a small minority are beneficial, yet over the long term these are essential for evolution by natural selection.
items.misconception: Most mutations are beneficial, because mutation is what drives evolution and makes organisms better adapted.
items.why: Mutation is presented as the raw material of evolution and evolution as improvement, so students conclude that mutations must generally be improvements. Popular culture (superheroes gaining powers from mutation) reinforces this. A random change to a working gene is far more likely to damage it or to make no difference than to improve it, so most mutations are harmful or neutral for the individual. Natural selection preserves the rare beneficial mutations and removes harmful ones, which is why mutation is essential for evolution in a species even though it is mostly bad news for an individual.
items.specStatementText: Mutation is where all new alleles come from
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a commercial genetic test show whether a person currently has a disease?
items.correct: No. It reads DNA variants and reports associations with potential future health and disease risk; it does not examine the person's current health.
items.misconception: A genetic test works like a blood test: a positive result means the person has the disease now.
items.why: Every other medical test students know (pregnancy tests, blood glucose tests, COVID tests) detects a present condition, so the word test is assumed to mean diagnosis. Direct-to-consumer marketing that promises to reveal your health encourages the same reading. Commercial genetic tests look for DNA variants that are statistically associated with future risk; they do not detect disease. A person can carry a risk variant and never develop the condition, or develop the condition without carrying any of the variants tested, which is one reason expert interpretation is needed.
items.specStatementText: Mutation is where all new alleles come from
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In a gene knockout, is it the gene or the protein that is inactivated?
items.correct: The gene: it is changed so that it is inoperative in every cell of the organism, so the protein is never produced. Blocking a protein with a drug or antibody is not a gene knockout.
items.misconception: A gene is knocked out by blocking or destroying its protein product in the organism, leaving the gene itself unchanged.
items.why: Students meet inhibitors and antibodies that stop proteins working, and the phrase knock out is used loosely for any loss of function. Because the phenotype in both cases comes from the protein being absent, the difference in what was changed is easy to miss. Gene knockout is defined by a change to the gene that makes it inoperative, so that no functional product is made in any cell and the change can be passed to the organism's offspring. This is what allows libraries of knockout organisms, each carrying a permanently inoperative gene, to be built and shared.
items.specStatementText: Knock a gene out to see what it does
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which component of the CRISPR–Cas9 system cuts the DNA?
items.correct: The enzyme Cas9. The guide RNA locates the target by base pairing but has no ability to cut DNA.
items.misconception: The guide RNA cuts the DNA at the point where it binds, and Cas9 holds the DNA in place.
items.why: The guide RNA is the component that is designed and discussed most, so students assign it the active role. Both components are described as working together, which blurs which does what. The guide RNA directs Cas9 to the target by complementary base pairing; Cas9 is the nuclease that cuts both strands of the DNA at that site. Neither component alone can edit a genome.
items.specStatementText: CRISPR–Cas9 cuts DNA where a guide RNA leads it
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If a genome edit is technically successful and does not harm the patient, is there still an ethical issue to address?
items.correct: Yes. Ethical issues such as consent, effects on future generations, fairness of access and the acceptability of altering human embryos remain even when the procedure works and is safe.
items.misconception: If a use of CRISPR works and is safe for the person treated, it is automatically ethical; ethical objections are just worries about safety.
items.why: In everyday reasoning ethical is equated with harmless, and school discussion of ethics in science is often reduced to risk. The success stories of CRISPR treatment make it seem that only technical problems stood in the way. The NOS point in this topic is that certain potential uses of CRISPR raise ethical issues that must be addressed before implementation. Editing embryos so that changes are inherited affects people who cannot consent, and the availability and purposes of editing raise questions of justice; these are not settled by showing that the method is safe.
items.specStatementText: CRISPR–Cas9 cuts DNA where a guide RNA leads it
